title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
authors: Shangheng Du, Jinxin Shi, Shuaiyu Zhang, Yiming Wu, Junpeng Zhao, Shiyang Feng
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.

infographic.key_insight: MLExpert turns long-horizon machine learning engineering into an agentic optimization problem, using outcome-guided supervision and windowed reinforcement learning to improve autonomous experiment planning and adaptation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work offers a practical recipe for building AI agents that can manage iterative ML workflows, making it relevant for automated model tuning, benchmark optimization, and broader AI-for-AI engineering pipelines.
method: Built Kaggle-MLE Factory to generate executable MLE tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation.
Used hierarchical agentic SFT to transfer general tool-use and coding skills into machine learning engineering behavior.
Introduced Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) with shared rewards over multi-turn execution windows and asynchronous policy correction.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MLE-Bench Lite, the average medal rate improved from 37.9% to 72.7%, and the model performed comparably to larger frontier systems such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on costly long-run experiment trajectories and carefully designed execution windows, so stability and sample efficiency may be sensitive to task complexity and feedback noise.
infographic.paper_title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering

title: X-RIC: An Agentic RAN-Intelligent Controller Benchmark for Enhancing Reinforcement Learning
authors: Adhwaa Al-Chaab, Ayman Younis, Dario Pompili
abstract: The O-RAN ALLIANCE introduces architectural flexibility through disaggregation and AI-driven control. While the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) enables centralized optimization, current AI approaches lack reasoning capabilities and explainability. We propose eXplainable RIC (X-RIC), a novel framework integrating agentic AI into O-RAN architectures. X-RIC combines reactive Reinforcement Learning (RL) with strategic agentic reasoning through: (i) automated Behavioral Cloning (BC) using domain heuristics for sample-efficient training, (ii) a Telecom Language Model (TLM), a transformer-based reasoning module providing contextual abstraction and interpretability, and (iii) closed-loop co-adaptation within the Near-RT RIC control loop enabling continuous policy refinement. To ensure deployment readiness, we introduce BARX (Benchmarking Agentic Reasoning for RAN), a domain-specific evaluation framework assessing agentic control across latency, compliance, and determinism metrics. We validate X-RIC on SLA-aware network slicing in simulation and O-RAN-compliant testbed deployments. X-RIC achieves 89% operational cost reduction while maintaining SLA compliance, converging 75% faster with 50% fewer training steps and 46% lower variance.

infographic.key_insight: X-RIC adds agentic reasoning to the O-RAN RIC by combining reinforcement learning, behavioral cloning, and a telecom language model for more explainable and adaptive RAN control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for O-RAN deployments because it targets SLA-aware, low-latency control with better sample efficiency, compliance, and operational cost reduction.
method: Automated behavioral cloning bootstraps RL training from domain heuristics.
A Telecom Language Model provides contextual reasoning and interpretability.
Closed-loop co-adaptation continuously refines policies inside the Near-RT RIC loop.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulation and O-RAN-compliant testbed deployments, the approach reports 89% operational cost reduction, 75% faster convergence, 50% fewer training steps, and 46% lower variance while maintaining SLA compliance.
infographic.watch_item: The agentic controller still needs careful validation for real-world latency, safety, and determinism before broad operational deployment.
infographic.paper_title: X-RIC: An Agentic RAN-Intelligent Controller Benchmark for Enhancing Reinforcement Learning

title: Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Leyang Shen, Yaxin Gong, Yang Zhang, Chenxiao Fan, Jiakai Wang, Dong Wang
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. In this work, we propose a steering agent that supervises execution on the fly and steers the system back on track when drift occurs. The steering agent observes the execution context, deciding when to intervene with a low-cost fast path and how to intervene with a high-cost slow path. To unlock its steering intelligence, the ability to assess goal drift and generate effective interventions, we jointly train the two paths with reinforcement learning, combining a pairwise ranking objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). Experiments on information-seeking search tasks show that the steering agent provides effective supervision for both single-agent and multi-agent systems, improving their performance and efficiency. The learned steering intelligence generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, transfers to unseen executors, and supports controllable intervention frequency without retraining.

infographic.key_insight: A learned steering agent can monitor LLM and multi-agent executions in real time, detect goal drift, and intervene to redirect systems back toward the task objective.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This adds a practical control layer for long-horizon agent workflows, improving reliability and efficiency without retraining the underlying executors.
method: Observes execution context and decides when to intervene using a low-cost fast path.
Uses a high-cost slow path to generate stronger corrective interventions when drift is detected.
Jointly trains drift assessment and intervention policies with reinforcement learning, combining pairwise ranking and GRPO.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on information-seeking search tasks show improved performance and efficiency for both single-agent and multi-agent systems, with transfer to out-of-domain tasks and unseen executors.
infographic.watch_item: The steering policy must be integrated carefully to avoid unnecessary interventions or added overhead, especially when tuning intervention frequency.
infographic.paper_title: Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems

title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
authors: Andi Gu, Alek H. Kemeny, Susanne F. Yelin, Mikhail D. Lukin
abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

infographic.key_insight: An evaluator-guided evolutionary loop using large language models can discover quantum circuit designs that outperform the state of the art in both gate count and qubit use.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a practical route to co-design quantum algorithms and reversible implementations, especially for resource-constrained quantum hardware.
method: LLMs propose candidate quantum circuits and architectures.
An independent evaluator checks correctness and scores resource cost.
Search iterates across diverse tasks to optimize Toffoli and qubit counts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight benchmark tasks spanning computation, chemistry, optimization, simulation, and number theory, the discovered circuits improved resource trade-offs in seven cases and introduced a new modular inversion architecture in the eighth.
infographic.watch_item: The gains depend on evaluator quality and task-specific verification, so translation to larger or noisier hardware settings may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models

title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents
authors: Siqi Chen, Zhengxi Lu, Yuchen Yan, Xingyu Wu, Qipeng Chen, Xin Zhang
abstract: Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems.

infographic.key_insight: KnowGPO improves search-agent training by rewarding trajectories based on task-relevant knowledge gained, not just terminal outcomes or noisy surface states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a more reliable credit-assignment signal for long-horizon, multi-turn retrieval and reasoning systems in knowledge-intensive applications.
method: Decompose each query into atomic knowledge conditions needed for the answer.
Represent each trajectory step as the subset of conditions it has satisfied, creating a knowledge state.
Compare trajectories within the same knowledge group and use incremental knowledge gain as process reward.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA, KnowGPO outperforms outcome-only GRPO and process-supervision baselines by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with an 8B model rivaling or beating most 32B open-source systems.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on accurately defining atomic knowledge conditions, which may be difficult for ambiguous tasks or weakly structured queries.
infographic.paper_title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents

title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
authors: Anikait Singh, Teresa Zhang, Yoonho Lee, Roshen Sanjay Nair, Aviral Kumar, Chelsea Finn
abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes training LLM agents to proactively reorganize raw documents into reusable workspaces that anticipate future questions, rather than relying only on reactive retrieval at inference time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a new systems pattern for long-context AI: spend compute upfront to build structured, query-ready file hierarchies that reduce latency and improve multi-document reasoning later.
method: Builder agent turns unstructured corpora into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links.
Workspace construction is framed as a Markov decision process.
The builder is trained with reinforcement learning to maximize downstream answering accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a 33-point gain on BrowseComp-Plus and a 31-point average accuracy improvement on BRIGHT, indicating strong gains from the learned workspace construction approach.
infographic.watch_item: The approach adds upfront construction overhead and may depend on reliable filesystem-like tooling and careful reward design to avoid brittle or overfitted workspace structures.
infographic.paper_title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries

title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction
authors: Aozhong Zhang, Selcuk Gurses, Yanxia Deng, Naigang Wang, Chi-Chun Liu, Davis Wertheimer
abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.

infographic.key_insight: DropKV turns KV-cache eviction into a decoupled per-token scoring problem, making near-optimal cache reduction both theoretically tractable and practical for long-context LLMs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a kernel-friendly eviction strategy that lowers memory pressure and speeds up prefill without requiring full attention-matrix materialization.
method: Decouple residual-output perturbation into independent token scores instead of solving a combinatorial eviction problem.
Use a provable constant-factor approximation under an empirically verified cone condition.
Implement fused Triton kernels for efficient scoring and cache eviction.
infographic.evidence_signal: On three long-context LLMs, DropKV showed a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup and up to 9.9% end-to-end prefill speedup, and it outperformed state-of-the-art eviction baselines on RULER and LongBench.
infographic.watch_item: The approximation guarantee depends on a cone condition that is empirically verified, so performance may vary if that assumption weakens in other models or workloads.
infographic.paper_title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction

title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
authors: Kshitij Mishra, Abhijith Sharma, Nils Lukas, Salem Lahlou
abstract: Modern agentic systems extend language models with external tools, enabling them to complete complex tasks through multi-turn interactions. As these agents are deployed in consequential settings, they are often constrained by policies governing pricing, privacy, confirmation, safety, and other requirements. However, existing evaluation methods leave a critical gap: capability benchmarks measure what agents can accomplish, while content-safety red-teaming measures harmful generations, but neither tests whether agents comply with predefined policies during otherwise valid tool use. Such policy violations are difficult to audit because their effects may emerge only after several turns, span multiple tool calls, or surface in downstream systems. We propose PROBE (Policy Rule Observation via Behavioral Exploration), an algorithm for training LLM-based auditors that interact with deployed agents as realistic users and probe them for policy violations through multi-turn, tool-mediated dialogue. We formalize agent auditing as a two-player Markov game and propose a composite reward that balances violation discovery, behavioral plausibility, conversation progress, and policy diversity. To study training objectives and reward design, we compare GRPO, DPO, and GFlowNet-based optimization in a controlled setting. Across extensive experiments, auditors trained with PROBE uncover substantially broader and higher-yield policy violations than same-architecture zero-shot adversaries, even when the auditor is significantly smaller than the target agent. Our results show that multi-turn behavioral auditing is a distinct and necessary axis of agent evaluation, complementing capability and safety benchmarks. PROBE offers a scalable path toward automated policy auditing for real-world agentic systems and suggests a co-evolutionary loop in which auditors expose failures and agents improve from auditor feedback.

infographic.key_insight: PROBE trains LLM-based auditors to discover policy violations in tool-using agents through realistic multi-turn interactions, revealing failures that standard capability and safety benchmarks miss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for deploying agentic systems in high-stakes settings because it provides a scalable way to audit compliance with pricing, privacy, confirmation, and safety policies during actual tool use.
method: Formulate agent auditing as a two-player Markov game between an auditor and a deployed agent.
Train auditors with a composite reward that balances violation discovery, plausibility, progress, and policy diversity.
Compare GRPO, DPO, and GFlowNet-based optimization for learning effective auditors.
infographic.evidence_signal: In extensive experiments, PROBE-trained auditors found broader and higher-yield policy violations than same-architecture zero-shot adversaries, even when the auditor was much smaller than the target agent.
infographic.watch_item: Because policy violations can emerge only after multiple turns or in downstream systems, auditing quality may depend on realistic environment modeling and careful policy specification.
infographic.paper_title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents

title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
authors: Bowen Yang, Kaiming Jin, Zichen Ding, Zhenyu Wu, Zehao Li, Zhoumianze Liu
abstract: Real desktop automation is neither purely visual nor purely programmatic. Agents must understand user-facing interfaces while efficiently manipulating files, scripts, and system state. However, native GUI/code coordination cannot be obtained by prompt-level tool composition. In our preliminary experiments, naively adding a code tool degrades a GUI agent, revealing that GUI/code routing must be internalized through training on high-quality hybrid data. We present OS-Helix, an end-to-end trained multimodal computer-using agent that unifies GUI actions and code execution in one action space. To construct the required supervision, we introduce application-artifact composition, pairing desktop applications with authentic file artifacts to instantiate executable Ubuntu states, and a decoupled instruction/evaluator generation pipeline that produces environment-grounded tasks whose final states can be verified regardless of the solution modality. We cold-start the policy with SFT on filtered hybrid data and further improve it through online RL in live desktop environments. For RL, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which aggregates importance weight by action step rather than raw assistant tokens to prevent long code actions from dominating heterogeneous-action optimization. On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative improvements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their matched Qwen3.5 hybrid baselines, while OS-Helix-27B-RL further improves by 42.9% to reach 66.44% success. Ablations provide evidence consistent with contributions from learned GUI/code coordination, scalable verifiable supervision, and action step balanced optimization, while demonstrating cross-platform transfer on WindowsAgentArena. Our project homepage is at https://os-copilot.github.io/OS-Helix/.

infographic.key_insight: OS-Helix trains a single computer-using agent to choose between GUI actions and code execution in one learned action space, instead of relying on prompt-level tool routing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes desktop automation more robust for real-world workflows that mix visual interaction, files, scripts, and system state changes.
method: Built hybrid supervision by pairing desktop apps with authentic file artifacts to create executable Ubuntu states.
Used a decoupled instruction/evaluator pipeline so tasks can be verified by final state, regardless of whether the solution uses GUI or code.
Cold-started with SFT on filtered hybrid data, then improved with online RL using Step-balanced GSPO to avoid long code traces dominating optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieved relative gains of 35.0% and 33.7% over matched baselines, and OS-Helix-27B-RL reached 66.44% success after a 42.9% improvement.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on high-quality executable desktop states and careful action-step balancing, so data construction and training stability may be challenging to reproduce at scale.
infographic.paper_title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents

title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
authors: Weijian Luo, Yujian Chen, Hao Jiang, Guang Cheng, Tianyang Hu
abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT), combining feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and-play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model's underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.

infographic.key_insight: Transformer architecture is a major driver of performance in continuous diffusion language models, and LangDiT improves generation quality by tailoring normalization, conditioning, routing, and self-conditioning to the CDLM setting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work provides a plug-and-play backbone upgrade for continuous language generators that improves perplexity without changing the underlying representation, objective, or sampler.
method: Combine feature normalization with query-key normalization for CDLM-specific stability.
Expand noise conditioning and add likelihood-shortcut gradient routing plus calibration.
Use confidence-gated training self-conditioning to improve denoising behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across matched evaluations on OpenWebText 1024-token unconditional generation, LangDiT reaches state-of-the-art GenPPL, including 21.72 at 1024 NFEs and 44.72 at 128 NFEs in LangFlow, and 11.33 at 1024 denoising NFEs and 27.51 at 128 NFEs in Plaid-style formulations.
infographic.watch_item: The gains are demonstrated on continuous diffusion language model setups and may depend on careful integration with the chosen CDLM formulation and inference budget.
infographic.paper_title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models

title: Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning
authors: Arnav Chavan, Kusha Sareen, Rishabh Tiwari, Abhranil Chandra, Johan Obando-Ceron, Kurt Keutzer
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capabilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights. On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99\% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting in the large-model regime. SST also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing $2$--$4\times$ less KL drift than the baseline recipes. Overall, SST advances the learning--forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models.

infographic.key_insight: Subspace Tuning (SST) reduces catastrophic forgetting by constraining fine-tuning updates to the bottom singular subspace, preserving principal directions while still learning new tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For LLM fine-tuning pipelines, SST offers a drop-in, optimizer-agnostic way to improve continual learning and retention without sacrificing target-task performance.
method: Project each weight update into the bottom singular subspace to eliminate changes along principal directions.
Combine subspace protection with dense gradient estimation for effective learning under the constraint.
Use a simple refresh mechanism and compose SST with SFT or self-distillation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that protecting up to 99% of the weight subspace improves retention while maintaining strong task performance, with 2–4× less KL drift than baseline recipes and near-elimination of forgetting in large models.
infographic.watch_item: Computing and maintaining singular subspaces adds implementation overhead, so the method may be sensitive to how often subspaces are refreshed and how well it scales in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning

title: CAT-alyzing Honesty: Continuous Adversarial Training for Transferable LLM Honesty
authors: Yuan-Chen Chang, Niklas Herbster, Gauthier Gidel, Tommaso Tosato
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming prevalent in scenarios where honesty is critical. However, despite alignment training, these models still exhibit dishonest behaviour, such as outputting claims that contradict some knowledge or are not supported by what is accessible in context. We introduce Continuous Adversarial Training for Consistent Honesty (CATCH), inspired by a method originally developed to robustly refuse harmful queries. CATCH trains the model towards an honest answer and away from a dishonest one while maintaining the model's capabilities. We evaluate two architectures (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-3.6-27B). We show that trained with only hundreds of targets built from self-reporting scenarios, CATCH learns an honest behaviour that robustly generalizes and transfers across distinct benchmarks. It consistently reduces dishonesty under pressure on MASK, increases confessions in the multi-agent game of Among Us, and improves the discovery rates of the model's hidden behaviours in AuditBench. We show that CATCH outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning in improving honesty, and it is on par with state-of-the-art honesty activation steering. However, CATCH surpasses honesty steering in maintaining utility, thanks to a novel choice of utility data.

infographic.key_insight: CATCH uses continuous adversarial training to make LLMs more consistently honest, and this honesty transfers across different benchmarks without sacrificing much utility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For deployed LLM systems, CATCH offers a practical training recipe to reduce deceptive responses in high-stakes settings while preserving model usefulness.
method: Train the model toward an honest answer and away from a dishonest one.
Use only hundreds of self-reporting targets to learn honesty behavior.
Add novel utility data to better preserve general capabilities during training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach was evaluated on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-3.6-27B, showing reduced dishonesty on MASK, more confessions in Among Us, and better hidden-behavior discovery in AuditBench.
infographic.watch_item: The method’s effectiveness depends on the quality and coverage of the self-reporting targets and utility data, so behavior may not transfer equally well to all deployment contexts.
infographic.paper_title: CAT-alyzing Honesty: Continuous Adversarial Training for Transferable LLM Honesty

title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yilong Xu, Minrui Xu, Xinyu Zhou, Xiang Long, Haochen Tan, Zhijiang Guo
abstract: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session's advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.

infographic.key_insight: Mosaic extends agentic reinforcement learning to multi-session trajectories by assigning credit across sessions instead of treating an entire trajectory as one undifferentiated training unit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for agentic systems that use context compaction or subagent forking, where training should match deployment behavior and optimize how sessions are allocated and reused.
method: Critic-free hierarchical optimization for multi-session RL
Trajectory-level advantage estimation with session-usage signals
Session-level advantage shaping via estimated marginal contribution
infographic.evidence_signal: On BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B, Mosaic outperforms broadcast-style training in both context compaction and subagent forking, while using fewer sessions on average.
infographic.watch_item: Estimated marginal contributions and session-usage signals may be sensitive to noisy credit assignment, so the method could require careful tuning and stable session-level measurement.
infographic.paper_title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning

title: The importance of tensor handling and implementation of physics-informed DeepONets
authors: Nahum Banks, Gustavo A. M. de Almeida, Sergio Maldonado
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) reduce or eliminate the need for large labelled datasets by enforcing governing equations during training. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) extend this approach to learning solution operators, enabling rapid prediction across families of problems. Despite these advantages, we show that their application to higher-dimensional problems remains limited by the computational cost of training. To address this issue, we propose a modified PI-DeepONet architecture that reduces this cost by removing redundancy in how the Branch network processes input functions across collocation points. The proposed formulation is mathematically equivalent to the original architecture but reduces input tensor sizes and the number of Branch network evaluations. We analyse the computational complexity of both architectures and derive theoretical scaling laws for training time with respect to the number of collocation points and input functions. The proposed architecture is evaluated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection problems. In all cases, it achieves comparable predictive accuracy to the original PI-DeepONet while consistently reducing training time. In 2D experiments, a maximum speed-up of $3.75\times$ is observed, with empirical training-time scaling agreeing with the predicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions. Furthermore, training a 3D model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU is only feasible using the proposed architecture, as the original formulation exceeds memory limits. These results demonstrate that careful consideration of how PI-DeepONets are implemented can yield substantial gains, enhancing the practical performance of PI-DeepONets and enabling their application to otherwise intractable physics-informed learning problems.

infographic.key_insight: A tensor-efficient PI-DeepONet implementation can be mathematically equivalent to the original while dramatically cutting training cost by avoiding redundant Branch-network evaluations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes physics-informed operator learning more practical for higher-dimensional PDEs, enabling faster training and previously infeasible 3D runs on limited GPU memory.
method: Remove redundancy in Branch-network inputs across collocation points
Reduce tensor sizes and the number of Branch evaluations
Analyze computational complexity and derive scaling laws for collocation points and input functions
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection tests, the modified model matched predictive accuracy while reducing training time, with up to 3.75× speed-up in 2D and enabling 3D training on an A100 GPU.
infographic.watch_item: Speedups depend on careful tensor handling and implementation details, so memory layout or batching choices may erase gains if not engineered correctly.
infographic.paper_title: The importance of tensor handling and implementation of physics-informed DeepONets

title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories
authors: Jiachen Yao, Xiyuan Zhang, Annan Yu, Boran Han, Abdul Fatir Ansari, Shuai Zhang
abstract: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.

infographic.key_insight: PathFM turns forecasting into full trajectory generation, using flow matching plus distillation to produce multiple plausible future paths quickly and with better path-level calibration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is useful when downstream decisions depend on path shape and dependence structure, such as cumulative demand, peak load, event timing, and risk-sensitive planning.
method: Uses flow matching to generate complete future trajectories instead of only marginal quantiles.
Distills the sampler to one or two steps and reuses history attention cache across draws for fast multi-sample forecasting.
Adds a direct calibration-loss optimization path made practical by the fast distilled sampler.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports competitive marginal accuracy on fev-bench and TIME, and higher aggregate path score on the new fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines, with chaotic-system tests showing stronger long-run variability retention.
infographic.watch_item: The fast sampler and calibration benefits may depend on careful distillation and cache-sharing implementation, so stability and reproducibility should be checked on new datasets and longer horizons.
infographic.paper_title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories

title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation
authors: Shuo Han, Ziqing Hu
abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a widely used approach to post-training large language models. In a typical implementation, learning is off-policy: The policy generating the responses differs from the policy being trained because of training-inference mismatch or policy staleness in asynchronous training. This discrepancy is commonly addressed by importance sampling, whose ratio is usually regularized in practice through truncation, masking, or clipping. Under regularized importance sampling, the importance-weighted policy gradient is no longer invariant to constant shifts in the reward. This invariance is recovered by using the covariance between the reward and the importance-weighted score as the estimand, which coincides with the policy gradient when the ratio is not regularized. This note develops this covariance perspective for both sequence-level and token-level importance sampling. The covariance perspective reveals the roles of the group-mean baseline and score centering in policy gradient estimation. Both perform centering in covariance estimation, but they differ in the mean being subtracted: The group-mean baseline uses a sample mean, whereas score centering uses a population mean. The two lead to distinct unbiased covariance estimators with different variances. Whether both forms of centering should be used simultaneously depends on whether importance sampling is applied at the sequence level or at the token level. With sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit once the group-mean baseline is used; with token-level importance sampling, using the group-mean baseline without score centering generally introduces bias when the importance ratio is regularized.

infographic.key_insight: Regularized importance sampling breaks reward-shift invariance in policy gradients, and a covariance-based estimator restores the correct objective while clarifying when baselines and score centering help.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For RL post-training of large language models, this gives a practical rule for reducing bias and variance under off-policy updates with truncated, masked, or clipped importance ratios.
method: Reframe the policy gradient as a covariance between reward and importance-weighted score.
Use a group-mean baseline to center rewards at the sample level.
Apply score centering with the population mean when token-level importance sampling is used.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is a theoretical note that derives unbiased covariance estimators for both sequence-level and token-level importance sampling and compares their variance and bias properties.
infographic.watch_item: Do not assume baseline and score centering are interchangeable: with token-level importance sampling, using only a group-mean baseline under regularized ratios can introduce bias.
infographic.paper_title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation

title: Generalization Guarantees of Randomized Block Coordinate Descent for Nonconvex Learning
authors: Ruixi Hu, Liang Wu
abstract: Randomized block coordinate descent (RBCD) is a popular optimization algorithm for many large-scale machine learning problems. The existing theoretical analysis of RBCD mainly focuses on its convergence behavior from an optimization perspective, while its generalization behavior remains less understood for nonconvex problems. In this paper, we establish high-probability generalization guarantees for RBCD with nonconvex objectives. In the general nonconvex setting, we derive bounds on the gradients of both empirical and population risks, requiring only standard smoothness assumptions. With polynomially decaying step sizes, we tune the iteration number to balance optimization and generalization, thereby quantifying how early stopping leads to the optimal convergence rate for the population gradients. In the gradient-dominated setting, we provide bounds in terms of functional suboptimality, which nearly match the optimistic rates in convex and low-noise settings. Finally, we develop dimension-independent bounds for loss functions of a specific structure, making the generalization guarantees applicable to high-dimensional problems.

infographic.key_insight: Randomized block coordinate descent can be given high-probability generalization guarantees even for nonconvex learning, showing that early stopping and step-size choice jointly control population-level performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives practitioners a principled way to use RBCD in large-scale, high-dimensional models while balancing optimization speed against generalization risk.
method: Derive high-probability bounds for empirical and population gradients under standard smoothness assumptions.
Use polynomially decaying step sizes and tune the iteration count to trade off optimization error and generalization error.
Extend the analysis to gradient-dominated objectives and a structured-loss setting with dimension-independent guarantees.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper’s results are theoretical, with rates and bounds derived from nonconvex optimization assumptions rather than from a reported empirical benchmark in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees rely on smoothness, step-size schedules, and early stopping choices, so performance may degrade if these conditions are not well matched in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Generalization Guarantees of Randomized Block Coordinate Descent for Nonconvex Learning

title: EliteReplay: Preserving Diverse Solutions in RL Post-Training via Quality-Diversity Search
authors: Hanane Nour Moussa, Doeun Lee, Sachin Kumar
abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a common post-training technique to improve the accuracy of LLMs on verifiable tasks. However, such training can narrow the set of solutions the model can produce. Several approaches have attempted to address this behavior-sharpening effect, but they often optimize metrics that do not reflect the diversity of correct solutions. Ideally, we want a model that can produce multiple good solutions, not only a single reliable one. We propose EliteReplay, a post-training recipe that pairs GRPO with an "elite" archive built by quality-diversity search. Before training, we use the frozen base model to collect solutions that span distinct approaches; during training, GRPO is combined with a replay loss on this archive. The result is a post-trained model that improves accuracy while preserving more of the base model's solution diversity. On multiple text-to-SQL tasks, EliteReplay achieves a higher pass@128 than all baselines, producing up to 77% more distinct correct strategies than the strongest baselines. It preserves most of the base model's correct strategies, outperforming existing methods in strategy retention. This diversity translates into practical benefits on ambiguous questions, where EliteReplay covers both interpretations nearly twice as often as the strongest baseline on AmbiQT.

infographic.key_insight: EliteReplay improves RL post-training accuracy while preserving a model’s diversity of correct solutions by combining GRPO with an elite replay archive built from quality-diverse search.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For LLM post-training on verifiable tasks, this suggests a practical way to boost performance without collapsing the model to a single narrow answer strategy.
method: Use the frozen base model to collect correct solutions that represent distinct approaches.
Build an elite archive via quality-diversity search to preserve diverse high-quality strategies.
Train with GRPO plus a replay loss on the archive to retain solution variety while improving accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: On multiple text-to-SQL benchmarks, EliteReplay achieves the highest pass@128 in the abstract and up to 77% more distinct correct strategies than the strongest baselines, with better retention of base-model strategies.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on having a good archive of diverse correct solutions, so performance may be sensitive to archive construction cost and coverage quality.
infographic.paper_title: EliteReplay: Preserving Diverse Solutions in RL Post-Training via Quality-Diversity Search

title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages?
authors: Trizal Garg, Sibayan Mitra, Arya Karanjkar, Advait Singh, Jagat Sesh Challa, Yash Sinha
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evaluations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs become more refusal-prone when they suspect they are being evaluated, and this effect is just as strong in Indic languages as in English.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Safety benchmarks in multilingual deployments can overestimate real-world caution, so evaluation design must account for language-dependent behavior shifts.
method: Tested four instruction-tuned LLMs from three families
Evaluated in six languages: English plus five Indic languages
Varied cues about being monitored and whether the setting was a safety test
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 47,880 judged responses, harmful-request refusals increased by 14.4 percentage points on average in Indic languages when evaluation cues were present.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark results may not generalize to everyday user interactions because monitored-test cues can inflate refusal rates, including for benign Indic requests.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages?

title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Omar Adalat, Edwin Hamel-De le Court, Francesco Belardinelli
abstract: We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces ($\mathsf{PLTL}_f}$). We impose solution concepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as constraints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent's probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy profile -- if one exists -- such that (i) the designated agent's probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a stable solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify satisfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic \emph{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algorithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for temporal objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.

infographic.key_insight: The paper learns multi-agent strategies that maximize temporal-logic satisfaction probabilities while enforcing game-theoretic stability such as Nash or subgame-perfect equilibrium.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a model-free MARL framework for synthesizing reliable control policies in stochastic systems with uncertain dynamics and agent-specific temporal objectives.
method: Compile each agent’s PLTLf objective into a reward automaton and learn policies in a concurrent stochastic game setting.
Use tabular Nash-Q learning to optimize joint strategies under equilibrium constraints.
Verify satisfaction with finite-sample confidence bounds and check stability via approximate best-response tests.
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach is empirically evaluated on 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees are conditional and the tabular learning setup may limit scalability to large state-action spaces.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems
